description: We're building Moon Crew, a free browser game where kids 7–12 run a base at the Moon's south pole and keep the crew alive by balancing life support, radiation shielding, power and food. Real NASA data runs it: BVAD life-support rates, archived DONKI solar flares and OSDR's Moon-soil plants. Play alone or as a crew of up to 4 at mooncrew.si. We love space, games and learning by playing. Our crew is set for this hackathon, but feedback from teachers, parents and space fans is welcome!
summary: Moon Crew is a free browser game where kids aged 7–12 run a small base at the Moon's south pole and keep its crew alive. Four needs compete: life support, radiation shielding, power and food. Three short missions put a real trade-off in the kid's hands: store sunlight in a second battery before a two-day night, or the habitat freezes (The Long Night); mine regolith to thicken the shield berm and, when a solar flare hits, ask Earth over a 1.3-second radio delay or act now (Storm Warning); and give each unit of water to breathing or to growing food (Thirsty Base). Every mission can be lost, and the debrief names the choice that decided it. NASA data runs the game: BVAD Rev 2 life-support rates, three real X-class flares of May 2024 from an archived NASA DONKI snapshot, and the Moon-soil plant finding of NASA OSDR study OSD-476, each with its source one tap away. Kids play alone or as a crew of up to four, on any phone, tablet or laptop, with no download and no account. Children are our hope to populate space: they need to understand the challenges ahead, and fall in love with them, together.
details:
Moon Crew is a free browser game where kids aged 7–12 run a small base at the Moon's south pole. Play it now at https://mooncrew.si (no download, no account; it opens https://mooncrew.klausos.com).

What it does

Moon Crew puts a kid in command of a small Moon base. A Moon day passes in a few minutes. Four meters (Life Support, Radiation Shielding, Power and Food) run down at rates scaled from NASA's BVAD Rev 2: oxygen, water and food per astronaut per day. To keep them up, the kid suits up and goes out with a mining laser: icy soil in a crater that never sees the Sun, regolith in a lava tube. They must get home before the suit's air runs low, then turn what they mined into water, oxygen, batteries or shield blocks at the Fabricator and in walk-in rooms (workshop, greenhouse, solar hut, bunk room). Every recipe costs power and time.

Mission mode: three missions with a real win and a real loss

• The Long Night (power): the Sun sets for two days. Build a second battery on Day 1 to store sunlight, or the habitat freezes.

• Storm Warning (radiation shielding and communication delay): mine regolith to thicken the berm. A solar flare comes on a random day with a 30-second warning. The kid can ask Earth for advice (1.3 s each way, so the answer arrives while the clock runs) or act now, then shelter behind the berm while the dose climbs toward a red line. The storm's strength comes from one of three real X-class flares of May 2024 (NASA DONKI, archived snapshot, labelled as such in the game).

• Thirsty Base (life support and food): ice becomes water, and each water goes either into life support or into a crop. With no harvest, the food runs out.

The debrief names the key choice. A win earns 1–3 stars by its margin, with a tip for the next star. The storm's day, hour and flare change every run.

Moonwalk mode: free play

Explore, dig, build and play with toys at your own pace. Nothing can go wrong, so younger kids can play too.

Survival mode: all four at once (1 player)

Air and water, shielding, power and food all run down together. Bring ice and regolith home, shelter from storms, and zap the made-up monsters off the buildings: every few days they come back tougher. The score is how many days the crew lasts, and the best run is kept.

Crew rooms

Up to four players open a room, share its link, pick a kid and a call sign (like Star-Hawk-20) and land together. No names, no chat, no accounts.

Made for ages 7–12

Icons come first, with one short sentence per fact. Every science fact sits behind a "?" with its source, and the About screen lists the data used. Terms are explained in context: the game says "Day", not "Sol", and explains what a dose is. Power, storage and yield numbers are labelled as game units, not NASA figures. The game's lines are also read aloud, for younger readers.

How it works

A static web app: HTML, CSS and JavaScript with the Canvas 2D API, the Web Audio API, and JSON data files (the BVAD rates, the DONKI snapshot, and every fact with its source). Progress stays in the browser. A small Node.js room server on Fly.io runs the crew rooms. It plays on phones, tablets and laptops, with touch or keyboard.

Why it matters

A kid doesn't just read that a Moon night is long: they lose a base to the cold and learn to store power first. Shielding becomes mass they dig. Water becomes a choice between breathing and eating. A radio delay becomes a decision under time pressure.

What's next

Portuguese and English for classrooms in Brazil and beyond, a little-crew mode for ages 4–6, this week's real solar flares from NASA DONKI on the storm card, and shared bases where friends keep one base alive together.

Tools

JavaScript, HTML5 Canvas, Web Audio API, Node.js and Fly.io; Python scripts for the art pipeline; headless Chrome, ffmpeg and HyperFrames for the demo video. Fonts: Fredoka and Nunito (SIL Open Font License).

How we used SI (Super Intelligence)

SI tools made most of Moon Crew's code and assets, directed by our team, who chose the challenge, made the design calls and picked every result. Everything SI-made is marked: the game shows a round "SI" badge on every screen, the demo video carries it for its whole length, the cover above carries it, and the game page's metadata, the audio files' tags and the video's tags say what was SI-generated.

• Code and texts: Claude Code (Anthropic; Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.2) wrote the game code and tests, the crew-room server, the art, animation and video pipeline scripts, and drafted the in-game texts from the cited sources. Every commit names the model. One helper script was written with Codex.

• Images: Codex image generation (OpenAI's Codex CLI in the ChatGPT app) made the still art: buildings, rooms, icons, items, toys, the lander, the logo, the grown-up citizens, the crew portraits and the comic-book cover. Our scripts keyed and cut them into sprites.

• Animation: the kid astronauts' move loops were generated with fal (MiniMax H3 Max reference-to-video, with Google Nano Banana edits for some start frames), then keyed into sprite sheets by our scripts. Helmets, gear and effects are drawn in code.

• Voice: ElevenLabs text to speech (Eleven v4) with stock voices: Jessica for the game, six others for the citizens, and Lily for the demo video's narrator. No real person's or child's voice was recorded.

• Music: Suno v6, instrumental, made on our Suno Premier plan. Sound effects are synthesized in code, with no recordings.

• Demo video and slides: real gameplay recorded in headless Chrome and edited with HyperFrames and ffmpeg; the slides were written with Claude.

No generated content uses NASA logos, flags or mission identifiers, and all characters are invented cartoons. Moon Crew uses NASA open data; it is not made or endorsed by NASA.
